t: Cao Xueqin began the novel in the 1740s and left it incomplete at his death in 1763 or 1764; it circulated in hand-copied manuscripts of eighty chapters until Gao E and Cheng Weiyuan printed a 120-chapter edition in 1791 and 1792.

Written in vernacular Chinese with the dialogue in Beijing Mandarin, it follows the fortunes of the Jia clan and the love of Baoyu, Daiyu and Baochai, and is known for its large cast and its female characters.
Scholars still dispute who wrote the last 40 chapters, and a field of study, Redology, grew up around the novel, its manuscripts and its lost ending.
dyk: The earliest manuscripts carry comments in red or black ink by unknown commentators, some of whom may have been members of Cao Xueqin's own family; the most prominent, Zhiyanzhai, revealed much about the original ending, which is now lost.
ev: Cao Xueqin begins composing the novel
The date of the Jiaxu manuscript, now in the Shanghai Museum
Gao E and Cheng Weiyuan publish the first printed edition, in 120 chapters
Wang Guowei publishes an essay that reads the novel through the philosophy of Arthur Schopenhauer
Hu Shih publishes Studies on A Dream of the Red Chamber, arguing that Gao E wrote the last 40 chapters
David Hawkes publishes the first volume of The Story of the Stone, the first eighty chapters in English for Penguin Classics
Yang Hsien-yi and Gladys Yang's complete translation, A Dream of Red Mansions, begins to appear in Beijing
Zhou Ruchang and Liu Xinwu produce a new 80-chapter version without the Cheng-Gao emendations

f.made: Cao Xueqin, a member of a prominent family that had served the Manchu emperors of the Qing dynasty and whose fortunes had begun to decline; the last 40 chapters of the usual 120-chapter text were edited and published by Gao E and Cheng Weiyuan
f.form: A novel in written vernacular (baihua), with dialogue in the Beijing Mandarin dialect and much poetry; 80 chapters in the earliest manuscripts, 120 in the Cheng-Gao printed edition, with nearly 40 major characters and over 400 others
f.where: The Jiaxu manuscript (1754) is in the Shanghai Museum, the Jimao manuscript (1759) in the National Library of China and the Gengchen manuscript (1760) in the library of Peking University; the novel is read in printed editions and translations
f.known: The Stone and the red dust; Jia Baoyu, Lin Daiyu and Xue Baochai; the Jia clan's decline; the Daguanyuan garden; the Rouge manuscripts and their commentators; Redology; the lost ending and the dispute over the last 40 chapters
